proposed_fields.title: Trump Pardons Former Border Patrol Agent Gary Mark Brugman
proposed_fields.description_short: Trump pardoned Gary Mark Brugman, a former Border Patrol agent convicted of violating a detainee’s civil rights.
proposed_fields.description_medium: The Justice Department’s clemency list records that Trump pardoned Gary Mark Brugman on December 23, 2020. It identifies a Western District of Texas conviction under the offense label “deprivation of rights under color of law,” with 27 months in prison and two years of supervised release. The Fifth Circuit’s opinion says Brugman punched and kicked a non-resisting detainee after the group complied with orders. The sources confirm the pardon and case facts, but not a documented motive for clemency.
proposed_fields.description_long: The Justice Department’s official list of pardons granted by Donald Trump records a full pardon for Gary Mark Brugman on December 23, 2020. It identifies his case in the Western District of Texas, the offense as deprivation of rights under color of law, a sentence of 27 months’ imprisonment, and two years of supervised release. In United States v. Brugman, the Fifth Circuit affirmed his conviction under 18 U.S.C. § 242. The court’s account says that after a group of detainees complied with orders to sit on the ground, Brugman punched and kicked a man who was not resisting. The White House clemency statement emphasized Brugman’s military and Border Patrol service and listed supporters of his pardon request; that is the administration’s rationale, not a judicial finding about the underlying conduct. The available records establish the pardon, offense, sentence, and conduct described by the court. They do not establish a private motive for Trump’s decision or any connection between the pardon and a specific benefit.
organization_tags: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit

uncertainty: No source establishes a private motive or quid pro quo for the pardon.

proposal.proposed_title: Village Voice reported on a 1988 inquiry into Trump Tower apartment financing
proposal.proposed_description_short: Wayne Barrett’s Village Voice investigation recounted an inquiry into two Trump Tower apartment purchases and Giuliani fundraising.
proposal.proposed_description_medium: The Village Voice’s 2019 archive republishes Wayne Barrett’s 1993 reporting on a federal inquiry into Trump Tower purchases by Robert Hopkins. Barrett wrote that agent Tony Lombardi interviewed Trump twice about the financing; weeks later, Trump publicly offered to raise $2 million for Rudy Giuliani if Giuliani ran for mayor. The article says Lombardi closed the inquiry, but the available record does not establish that the pledge caused the decision or prove money laundering.
proposal.proposed_description_long: Wayne Barrett’s Village Voice investigation, originally published in 1993 and republished in 2019, examined a 1988 federal inquiry into the financing of two Trump Tower apartments purchased by Robert Hopkins. Barrett reported that Hopkins struggled to document income, that Trump signed a bond connected to Hopkins’s deposit, and that agent Tony Lombardi conducted two hour-long interviews with Trump about the sale. Within weeks, the story says, Trump announced he could raise $2 million if then-U.S. Attorney Rudy Giuliani ran for mayor; Trump later co-chaired a Giuliani fundraiser. Barrett reported that Lombardi closed the inquiry without assigning it a case number, and the Village Voice editor frames that closure as a favor to Trump. This is an attributed investigative account, not a reproduced federal case file or court finding. It supports an entry about what the Village Voice reported and the sequence it described, not a conclusion that Trump committed money laundering or that fundraising caused Giuliani or Lombardi to end an investigation. Later articles cite Barrett’s original reporting; they do not independently corroborate every allegation.

proposal.description_long: KFF’s July 23, 2025 analysis of the enacted reconciliation package reports the Congressional Budget Office’s estimate that the law would reduce federal Medicaid spending by $911 billion over a decade, after accounting for overlaps among provisions. The original title and synopsis combine a spending projection with claims of realized service cuts, re-institutionalization, and a causal connection to federal action. Those claims require separate state-level evidence and are omitted here. This correction attributes the projection to KFF’s presentation of CBO estimates, preserves the ten-year horizon, and avoids implying that the spending estimate alone proves particular service losses or outcomes for people with disabilities.

proposed_fields.title: Trump Said Arizona Officials Were Trying to Steal the 2022 Election Amid Tabulator Problems
proposed_fields.description_short: Trump said Arizona officials were trying to steal the election after Maricopa County reported ballot-machine problems.
proposed_fields.description_medium: On November 8, 2022, Donald Trump posted that Maricopa County voting machines were not counting ballots and said, “They are trying to steal the election with bad Machines and DELAY.” Reuters reported printer and tabulator problems at some vote centers. A judge rejected a request to extend voting hours, finding no evidence that voters had been prevented from casting ballots. The equipment failures do not establish fraud or a stolen result.
proposed_fields.description_long: During Election Day on November 8, 2022, Maricopa County reported problems with ballot-on-demand printers and tabulators at some vote centers. Donald Trump used the reports to make a specific public accusation. In a post that afternoon he said some machines were not counting votes, then wrote: “People of Arizona: Don’t get out of line until you cast your vote. They are trying to steal the election with bad Machines and DELAY.” Reuters reported the machine problems and the fraud claims made by Trump and other election deniers. In a related court proceeding, a judge rejected a Republican request to extend polling hours because the party had not shown that voters were prevented from casting ballots. Maricopa County’s post-election report documents equipment problems and how ballots were handled; those problems are not evidence that votes were changed or that the election was stolen. The original title’s reference to midterm losses is misleading because Trump’s cited post was made before the results were known. This draft records the statement and the verified dispute without endorsing its allegation.

uncertainty: Trump’s post is an allegation, not proof of fraud; it preceded final results, so “midterm losses were stolen” misstates the timing.
